power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. info.title: A set of dynamical rules for conversational progression act as a precursor to collective cognition

text.text: Conversation unfolds between speakers as a series of coordinated updates from prior ideas expressed in earlier utterances to new sets of ideas.

This process of speakers and conversation partners jointly updating prior "conversation states" is an important piece of the cognitive scaffolding that enables social coordination, and even collective cognition -the capacity for individuals to pool their cognitive resources to solve problems together.
However, a functional data-driven description of how this process works is missing in the extant literature.

This report provides a functional description of how conversation states are updated in terms of information-theoretic processes, while analyzing a corpus of 5,448 conversations in nine typologically diverse languages.
Our results show that individuals form a strongly connected distributed computational system during conversation, which generates new information according to a power-law distribution.
These properties of conversation may be the foundation upon which human interaction encodes and solves a potentially unbounded number of problems and ideas.

Significance statement: While a number of studies take for granted that conversation acts as a kind of complex dynamical system for social coordination, the literature lacks a foundational, function-centered, computational description of how conversation facilitates this.

The current study leverages one of the largest collections of conversation data to date, compiled from several massive corpus projects, to root conversational progression in information-theoretic principles.
Our results offer a new foundation that connects several research programs in the language sciences and enables new formal theoretical development.

text.text: We can observe the outcomes of collective cognition in a number of speaker-partner behaviors including: (1) alignment in speakers and partners' linguistic features [21, 22]; (2) formation of complementary behaviors during interaction [23] [24] [25] [26]; and in (3) periodic structure of sentence-level entailments between adjacent utterances [27].

text.text: These diverse patterns of coordination may be undergirded by a set of principles that characterize an underlying system that organizes interaction.
Diverse collaborative behaviors would emerge from that system's organizing principles, yet the present literature lacks a quantitative model that may serve as this foundation.
This missing piece is an important bridge that would synthesize how interaction builds in a turn-by-turn manner into larger coordinative behaviors.

Because each contributor of new ideas in a conversation is a unique individual, and because the outcomes of their interaction are shared, how people collaborate to build on prior concepts should exhibit principles of distributed computation -when separate, unique components work together to form a singular computational system.

Naturally occurring distributed computation has two important features: (1) power-law, or fractal scaling * † in their outputs [30, 31], and (2) demonstrable mutual influence across the components of the system [30].

text.text: Thus, we hypothesize that conversation, as a dynamical system that facilitates speakers' and partners' building on prior concepts, exhibits these two traits.

text.text: Ergo, if we start from some prior utterance (x), we can calculate how much information is required to move from the ideas in it to any subsequent utterance (y).

If each turn by speakers or CPs uniquely generates new information [2, 4, 6], but needs to be related to prior turns in order to support computation [30, 31], then the way information accrues across turns should exhibit properties of distributed computation.

text.text: This forms a fundamental constraint on how information accrues over conversation in order to maintain its utility as a mechanism for joint reasoning processes, broadly and irrespective of specific task structure.
We look here for evidence of distributed computation in the current study.
The current study analyzed patterns in how, given any random starting point in a conversation, speakers add new information to build on prior idaes.

We applied a novel information-theoretic and language-modeling framework for big data to a massive dataset of 5448 conversations compiled from dozens of naturalistic corpora of people engaging in normal conversations.

Our results demonstrate that conversation can provide a vital medium for distributed, universal computation where parties generate information via moving away from prior ideas in ways that allow for infinite -i.e., universal -variability.
We use convergence-information (CI) [35, 36] to calculate the information how much speakers moved away from the ideas expressed in an earlier utterance x when expressing a current utterance y.
text.formatted: We use convergence-information (CI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36]</ref> to calculate the information how much speakers moved away from the ideas expressed in an earlier utterance x when expressing a current utterance y.

text.text: CI uses a large language model to convert utterances x and y to sets of token level embeddings (i ∈ x and j ∈ y) representing the meaning of each token (equation 1), and then uses the distance between the token embeddings for each token i ∈ x and their nearest neighbor in j ∈ y to calculate a probability that the meaning of a word in x exists in y (equation 2).
This probability is then converted to Shannon information (equation 3).

To calculate the proportion of total information that a speaker has contributed when building on the ideas expressed in x, we calculate the CDF of the speakers cumulative contributions to the conversation -the proportion of the integral for subsequent utterances y ∈ Y , ∆ t turns after the very first utterance y spoken by a speaker or one of their CPs.
Where T contains all values ∆ t ∈ T for a single speaker or CP's contributions after the utterance x.

To calculate scaling dynamics in how people accrue information over time, we regress the log-log transformed CDF to the difference in time from a speaker or CP's first contribution after x to the current turn: log CDF (∆ t ) ∼ β 0 + α log ∆ t where α is the power-law scaling exponent [37, 38].

Complexity-matching tests whether or not two dynamical series data match eachother's behavior as they evolve [39].

As a second test of coordination, we calculate the average Lyapunov exponent (λ) for the difference in information generated by speakers building on their own prior utterances x and each of their CPs building on x, between utterances closest to eachother in time.

Lyapunov exponents (λ) distinguish between three dynamical behaviors: (1) λ < 0 speakers and CPs converge on generate similar amounts of information as time progresses; (2) λ > 0 speakers and CPs diverge in amounts of information generated; and (3) λ ≈ 0 speakers and CPs are strongly locked (though different) in how much information each generates.

Parametric tests indicate that the scaling behavior of individuals engaging with one another is only weakly different (∆(α sp(x) ; α sp(x) = -.018, t(4743) = -2.28, p = .01).

Across conversations, languages, and language families, we find that (1) speakers and their partners accumulate new information according to a fractal power-law order parameter, (2) this information accrual rate arises from speakers engaging in their immediate conversational context, and (3) speakers appear to coordinate their rates of information accrual, with speakers generating new information relative to their own utterances at a slightly faster, more "critical" rate than CPs, but CPs being in sync with them in their own information generation behavior.
Though, evidence for coordinated differences in speaker and CP behavior is only weakly powered.

Indeed, in the crosslinguistic study, which, while leveraging a smaller number of examples, encompasses greater diversity in human participants and behaviors, complexity matching appears to be more likely than synergy.
An important implication of the fractal power-law exponents is that conversations tend to be more orderly (i.e., less information dense) for turns that are closer to a particular reference point.

This tendency points towards a tendency for humans to communicate in a way such that turns in close proximity are more related to one another semantically, and that similarity isn't inherently stable or uniform across time.
Pick any turn and speakers will generate, or "pack", the most information density in latter turns.
Power-law scaling, and especially fractal powerlaw scaling, allows for non-normative starting points in the amount of information people generate, even in close proximity to an initial utterance x.
What does this mean?
There may not be a characteristic rate of information that one contributes to a conversation right after an utterance x is proclaimed.
That can vary.
But the behavior of adding information -less early on, and rapidly increasing before leveling off -is consistent across speakers.
The dynamics are shared, even if the initial amount of information contributed varies.
The presence of power-law scaling, context specificity, and coordinated behavior all hint towards speakers working together as a kind of distributed computational system.
Distributed computation occurs when multiple interacting components can work together to "compute" outputs across a universal set of possible problems [30, 31].
text.formatted: Distributed computation occurs when multiple interacting components can work together to "compute" outputs across a universal set of possible problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31]</ref>.

text.text: Such systems in nature require (1) power-law scaling (which allows outputs to vary in initial values but to scale in predictable ways, supporting computation over an infinite number of possible problems [28, 29, 41, 42]) and (2) demonstrable coordination between the components of the system.
text.formatted: Such systems in nature require (1) power-law scaling (which allows outputs to vary in initial values but to scale in predictable ways, supporting computation over an infinite number of possible problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42]</ref>) and (2) demonstrable coordination between the components of the system.

text.text: Conversation meets both of these criteria.
Thus, conversation can provide the requisite scaffolding for collective cognition.
Framing conversation as optimized for generating and compounding new information provides a scaffolding linking a number of potentially contradicting prior theories.

For example, while Interactive Alignment Theory (IAT: [21, 22]) predicts that speakers will increasingly align on shared linguistic and cognitive structures regardless of all other factors, Communication Accommodation Theory (CAT: [43, 44]) predicts that alignment is modulated according to social and cognitive goals.

text.text: Interpersonal Synergy (IS: [23] [24] [25] [26]) contradicts IAT as well, positing that people tend to form compensatory behaviors rather than just aligning.

text.text: Other work appears to indicate that alignment at the level of the semantic entailments for whole, adjacent utterances has a periodic structure, contradicting all three theories above [27, 45].

text.text: All of these behaviors, however, can be linked from the current perspective.
If conversation is (functionally) a tool for compounding information, then each of these theories is a different outcome of more general information generation processes.
A universal pattern in how information accumulates across languages points to a possible, usage-based "linguistic universal".

Linguistic universals are typically posited to be universal grammatical features shared across languages [46], though they are quite rare [47], and empirically validated universals tend to be either pragmatic [48, 49] or arise from clear biological constraints [50].

text.text: The current results are indeed more pragmatic, and tell us nothing about grammatical structures of the languages surveyed.

But if language in communication is optimized for coordinating how speakers and CPs generate new information, then various groups can be left to evolve varied linguistic features and norms based on the immediate needs of those communities [51, 52].
text.formatted: But if language in communication is optimized for coordinating how speakers and CPs generate new information, then various groups can be left to evolve varied linguistic features and norms based on the immediate needs of those communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52]</ref>.

text.text: This does not necessarily contradict generative approaches either, as observed (versus possible) features likely arise from human cognitive constraints.
While we present evidence that power-law rules discussed here are widespread, their genesis is opaque.
Did humans evolve to innately generate power-law distributed outputs during communication?
Or is this a learned behavior that develops as children age?
Future studies could look to longitudinal development of information generation processes in children as a possible way to answer this question.
There are further limitations to the findings described here.
For example, while in aggregate there is a tendency for particular values for powerlaw exponents, there is still variation.
What might cause that variance?
Perhaps differences in context trigger subtle differences in the rules we uncovered?
The current study answers questions about aggregate phenomena, but these finer-grained questions remain unaccounted for.
The current work is focused exclusively on understanding dynamical patterns in conversation -i.e., in multiparty interactions.
But contemporary research shows that monologic, intra-personal communication shares many of the same attributes of dialog [53, 54].
text.formatted: But contemporary research shows that monologic, intra-personal communication shares many of the same attributes of dialog <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54]</ref>.

text.text: While outside of the current paper's scope, future work should look at the similarities (and differences) between dialogic and monologic communication.
What is shared (and what differs) between the two will likely tell us important information about the cognitive constraints that structure both.
Ludwig Wittgenstein proposed that communication be cast as a kind of game [55].
text.formatted: Ludwig Wittgenstein proposed that communication be cast as a kind of game <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref>.

text.text: That metaphor for the process of working together during conversation has influenced decades of research into human communication since.

If the objective of conversation is to extend the cognitive processes of its participants, however, that game might look a whole lot more like a group of friends building with Legos together -riffing off each other's prior contributions, and borrowing pieces of various levels of completion to build something interesting and novel to give back to the group as a kind of intellectual gift for others to play with.
Even in such an open-ended game, however, certain rules help structure the way individuals work together.
We hope that this paper provides an interesting first look at what those rules actually look like during conversation.
How does one identify power-law changes in information being generated during the course of a conversation?
A number of a priori choices about how to represent the temporal dimension of a conversation need to be made in order to effectively measure this.
We decided on the following: It is not clear the degree to which speakers experience the passage of time per se during conversation.
Nor did we have access to time-stamped data in all cases.
We thus opted to represent time in terms of the number of turns having occurred prior to some utterance.
Thus, if a speaker produces a turn after 20 turns have already occurred, the measurement t for that turn is 21.
Temporal distance, or ∆ t , between any two turns is thus the number of turns between two utterances.
Notably, conversations occur between two or more speakers in our data.
This also poses an interesting problem.
What is an appropriate measurement of distance when attempting to analyze conversations for what may be powerlaw distributed effects?
In the current study, we wanted to know the degree to which information changes from one speakers' first utterance y after some utterance x to their next utterance y after x.
Our hypothesis is that changes in information will scale according a power-law the farther apart the first utterance y is from the next utterance y, for each speaker in a conversation.

So, for example, if we are testing how easily we can recover the semantic content some prior utterance x at time t = 1, a speaker's (or conversation partner, p) first utterance after x occurs at time t = 4, and their next utterance occurs at time t = 7, then ∆ t for that speaker moving from their first turn to their next turn is ∆ t = 7 -4 = 3.
If their next utterance occurs at time t = 10, then ∆ t = 10 -4 = 6.

This distinction treats each combination of speakers -the speaker having spoken the first utterance, x, and the speaker having spoken some subsequent utterance(s) y -as unique time-series in the data.
Our hypotheses, thus, center on the idea that information scales according to a power-law as ∆ t increases in each time-series.
We denote an utterance y spoken by some speaker s as y s .
An example conversation demonstrating how we partition time is included in figure 1a.

text.text: One last note: prior work has shown that utterances made by the same speaker who spoke the utterance x (self , or formally sp(x) = sp(y)) tend to generate less new information in more temporally proximal turns, but scale much faster in how much information they generate, when compared to utterances spoken by one of their conversation partners in the same conversation (conversation partners, p, or formally sp(x) ̸ = sp(y)).
We thus differentiate between the two conditions using the above mentioned annotations.

text.text: We focus in this paper on CI.
CI uses a large language model (LLM) to convert two utterances (x and y) into a series of embeddings for each token in those utterances (for all tokens i ∈ x and j ∈ y; see equation 5).

It then compares every token i ∈ x to tokens j ∈ y to find the embedding in y that is closest to the embedding for the token i in the utterance x in that embedding space (measured using Cosine Error, or CoE).

It then converts the distance between the token i ∈ x and its nearest neighbor in y to a probability (equation 6), and then asks how much Shannon information [32] is required to reconstruct the utterance x using those nearest neighbors (equation 7).

Importantly, α is characteristic of how information accumulation behaves.
When α ≈ 0, information accumulates in an unpredictable, unorderly way regardless of time.
This means that some early parts of the CDF could jump well beyond what we would expect even logarithmically of later changes to the CDF.
When ||α|| ≈ 1, information accumulation scales linearly over time.

Often, this is due to Gaussian random processes, where each addition of information is "randomly" sampled from a simple Gaussian distribution and thus each new addition of information is approximately equal to the last contribution.
Notably, when ||α|| > 1, this indicates that information accumulates slowly at first but then rapidly increases as time progresses.

text.text: It is worth noting that each speaker might contribute a new utterance at varying lengths of time after their first utterance.
For example, a speaker might contribute an utterance at time t = 4, and they may not speak again until some 20 turns later at time t = 24.

Given that we calculate an integral for each time series, large variations in time between subsequent utterances can potentially bias our results towards fractal scaling if they are not controlled for in some way-there may be huge stretches in time where it seems like information accrual is utterly stagnant.

While that would yield exciting results for our study-we are precisely interested in whether or not information accrues according to a fractal pattern as a necessary condition for supporting distributed computation and thus collective cognition-that result would likely be an artifact of our analytical method rather than a genuine result.

Instead, we integrate our data according to how many utterances in the series for the speaker-CP pair has passed thus far, and then leverage the difference in time ∆ t as an index for how much of the integral is "available" at that point in time.
This works because there is an exactly bijective mapping between the number/index of an utterance in some series and its ∆ t .

If a speaker contributes three utterances -one at time t = 4, another at time t = 13, and another at time t = 20 -then the amount of information that that speaker has contributed by their second turn at time ∆ t = (13 -4) = 9 is the total amount of information in the integral after their second turn.

While this "squishes" the distribution for the integral significantly in some ways, it biases our results towards a null result rather than fractal scaling outright, either making the integral appear more linear/Gaussian than it actually is over time, or more chaotic if there is no characteristic slope to how the CDF scales.

For the current study, CI is useful in assessing how much more information is required to move back to the set of semantic structures contained in an utterance x when starting from the semantic structures contained in any subsequent utterances y ∈ Y .
When this value is high, it requires more effort to go back to the structures in x from those contained in y.
When it is low, it means that the semantic structures in x have carried over in time into the set of semantic structures contained in the utterance y.
Furthermore, our interest is in how much information scales in speakers' subsequent utterances compared to an utterance x, for each specific speaker of utterances y.

So, for a conversation where there are two or more speakers, each utterance y can be spoken by either (a) the same speaker as the speaker of the utterance x (denoted sp(x) = sp(y)), or by any one of the speakers of x's other conversational partners (sp(x) ̸ = sp(y)).
To denote information generated by a specific speaker, we use the following notation: I(x; y p ) where p indicates the p th speaker/conversation partner in the conversation.

For each utterance x we calculated the accumulation of information for each speaker who contributed an utterance y after x by calculating the cumulative density function (CDF) of information for each of their subsequent utterances.
The CDF was calculated using the proportional integral of total information up to some time ∆ t after the first utterance spoken by some speaker (sp(y)) was first contributed after the utterance x.

As an illustration, if one speaker (sp(y)) generates three utterances after x, we calculate the CDF for how much information they have contributed out of all the information they will contribute up to that point for the first utterance, the second utterance, and then the third utterance.
This allows us to quantify the density of how much information speakers will contribute has accumulated over time.
The CDF for each speaker represents the proportion of total information that they will thus contribute to the conversation after some utterance x.
There is a useful and intuitive way to think about how the integral over total information is operating in this instance, and how that relates to power-law and fractal scaling.

If one drew an x and y axes on a piece of paper, where the x-axis is the number of turns between the first turn spoken by a speaker or CP after x and a current turn being measured, and the y axis is the amount of information for the comparison of the utterance x to the utterance y at that point (i.e., ∆ t ), the integral gives the total amount of the paper covered/under the curve up to that value of ∆ t .
The proportional integral shrinks the size of that paper to a single cube.

The scaling exponent in this measurement regime, thus, tells us the expected total mass of the distribution up until that point, and fractional scaling here indicates that the mass curves in on itself in a way that is fractal or scale-free.
